utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everyone. I'm not going to ask anyone to introduce themselves because we have the same people present as yesterday. The Trial Chamber will issue a number of rulings today because, as I announced yesterday, we had a working meeting this morning, and I'm now in a position to issue a number of rulings, and this will be done orally. The first ruling has to do with the computer. We took note of what was said yesterday by Mr. Praljak, and we also took note of the four letters, the last being dated 16th of August, a letter addressed to OLAD and related to that issue. We instructed the legal officer of the Chamber to take -- to get in touch with OLAD very quickly in order to inform us if it will be feasible for the computer to have bigger memory. As far as I know, it should not cause any technical problems apparently, and the cost is about a few euros, but there are a number of procedures that have to be followed at the UN in order to purchase that and that might explain the delay. In any case, we've asked the legal officer to get this information as quickly as possible, and as soon as we get this information I'll let Mr. Praljak know what's going on and what's going to happen. And I hope that you will very quickly obtain what you're requesting, because this a perfectly legitimate request. Now, in relation to the documents mentioned by Mr. Murphy yesterday, we believe that at the end of the cross-examination the Prosecution, if it wishes to do so, will be able to tender a motion for the -- to issue -- to file a motion for the admission of these documents. The Defence will respond in line with our previous decision and then we'll rule on whether these documents should be admitted or not. At this stage, the Judges of the Chamber believe that the accused have not suffered any prejudice because the Defence is still in a position to ask appropriate questions to the witness based on documents that the Defence has received for quite some time now. We have another decision in relation to the exhibits in relation to Witness Manolic. I'm going to read this decision out very slowly for everybody to listen very carefully. The Trial Chamber has to rule about the admission of exhibits tendered by the parties as part of the testimony of Mr. Josip Manolic. The Trial Chamber would like first to recall that in line with the decision of the 13th of July on the admission of evidence, when a party only introduces an excerpt of an exhibit during the hearing it should only request the admission of this particular excerpt. The Chamber invites the party to file in writing before the 30th of August the list of exhibits submitted to the witness Manolic that the parties would like to see admitted. We would like to recall that as far as the excerpts are concerned, the parties are to provide the page numbers or the paragraph numbers of the relevant exhibits. Secondly, as for the admission of the exhibits in the testimony of Mr. Josip Manolic, since this is -- this happened before the decision rendered on the 13th of July, the Trial Chamber is ready to consider any decision filed by the Prosecutor in case the Prosecutor wants to file -- want to tender the exhibits that were not submitted to the witness. This motion should be filed before the 30th of August and should include the necessary reasons provided for in the guidelines for the admission of evidence. The Defence will then have eight days to respond and to raise any objections it might have for each of the exhibits tendered for these exhibits to be admitted. Last decision rendered orally today. This has to do with the exhibits and the evidence in relation to Mr. Omer Hujdur. By oral ruling rendered today, the Trial Chamber rules on the admissibility of evidence related to the testimony of Omer Hujdur, who was heard on the 20th and 21st of June, 2006. The Trial Chamber has decided to admit the following exhibits submitted by the Prosecution because of their probative value and their relevance to a certain extent: P 01542, P 01564, P 01656, P 03020, P 03907, P 04247. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber has decided to admit the following exhibits tendered by the Defence because of their probative value and their relevance: 2D 00055, 2D 00056, 3D 00046, 3D 00126, 3D 00131, 3D 00287, 3D 00289, 3D 00291, 3D 00292. However, the Trial Chamber has decided not to admit the following exhibits tendered by the Defence because considering their contents or, rather, because the witness had no knowledge of their existence or their contents. These are exhibits 3D 00123, 3D 00125, 3D 00136, 3D 00138, 3D 00284, 3D 00285, 3D 00290. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber has decided not to admit the following Defence exhibits because the Trial Chamber is not satisfied of their -- about their authenticity or their contents: 2D 00154 -- no, there is a mistake. 2D 00054, 3D 00048, 3D 00049, 3D 00050, 3D 00122, 3D 00136, 3D 00137. Finally, the Trial Chamber has decided not to admit the following exhibits submitted by the Defence because these exhibits had not been presented or because it was not possible to present these exhibits to the witness Hujdur during the hearing, these are exhibits 3D 00130, 3D 00286, 3D 00288. Since the decision on the admission of evidence related to Witness Hujdur has been issued today, in other words, after the decision on the admission of evidence that was rendered on the 13th of July, 2006, the Trial Chamber decides or rules that the same principles should apply to this decision, the principles that were outlined in the decision on the 13 -- of the 13th of July, 2006. Therefore, in line with this decision, the Trial Chamber makes it possible for the Prosecution to file a motion with the Chamber if the Prosecution wishes to tender additional evidence, evidence that was not submitted to Witness Hujdur, and such a motion should be filed on the 30th of August, 2006 at the latest, and it should state the appropriate reasons for its filing following the guidelines for the admission of evidence. The Defence will have eight days to respond and to make objections for each of the exhibits submitted and tendered through the motion. This is the end of these decisions. We are now going to move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're in open session. I'm now going to give the floor to the Defence counsel who will proceed with the cross-examination of the witness. I don't know whose turn is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. On the 65 ter chart we received, our client's name was not marked and we don't have the names of these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis, what can you say to that? What can you respond to Mr. Ibrisimovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm not -- in all honesty, Your Honour, I'm not sure I understand Mr. Ibrisimovic's concern. Is it the fact that the 65 ter chart did not mention his client's name and, therefore, he doesn't have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Ibrisimovic, can you please clarify your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there was a misinterpretation, Your Honour. When my learned friend disclosed the chart for this witness, he left out the name of our client. As there was no mention during the examination-in-chief of our client, I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Following the counsel -- Mr. Karnavas was back on his feet. He sat back again and now he's on his feet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, Mr. President and everyone in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Beese. I want to go back to the one document that was referenced earlier. I take it your position is you wish to be going into private session when I make reference to that document, you personally? I know the Court's ruling on that, but is your personal wish to treat that document as something that we should not be talking about in open court?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I take it before coming here today, and perhaps even overnight, you've had a chance to look over any documents to refresh your memory, any that were generated by others or those generated by yourself?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. The question was: Have you refreshed your memory? I know they're available, because obviously you have them. And if you generated them, obviously they would be in your possession. The question is did you review them to refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, first I want to start with the mission itself, and we'll start from there. As I understand it, you got involved with ECMM at or about January 2nd, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you remained in that motion until approximate July 21, 1993.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you arrived in country or in theatre, as you put it, somewhere, I believe, on the 8th of January.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And barring two -- two times that you -- that you were absent on vacation, and I believe there might have been two weeks or 10 days at a time, that entire period you were in country or in theatre; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. The total amount of time that you spent in -- in the mission, would that be six months?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated to us in being questioned by the Prosecutor that the turnover was rather high in the ECMM mission.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that was because some countries would -- would allow for their observers or monitors to be there for as little as four months, and in the UK's position was as long as two years, but it varied; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Some monitors like yourself were new to the region; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it would be fair to say that those who were new to the region and new to the conflict came with more or less a tabula rasa, a blank slate other than what they might have read in the newspapers, in the press, or perhaps a book they might have read in getting ready for the mission?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that was pretty much your case as well?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I hope I'm not speaking too fast for the translators. I'll slow down. We speak the same language, so I need to slow down a little bit. Now, in this particular case, you've told us that you were not a student of the HDZ or the HVO. It's in your transcript. I can get it. But in this particular case, it's fair to say that you knew little, very little, of the former Yugoslavia itself; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're not a history buff, and not history buff of this particular region; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not of this particular region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you had not studied in any significant way the former Yugoslavia, at least it's political set-up; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Nor had you looked at its constitution prior to the break-up?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Or subsequent to the break-up?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as you well know, as Yugoslavia was breaking up and as these new republics were being recognised, they were -- in doing so, they were forming their own constitutions as legitimate states recognised by the UN; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so again, prior to your arrival and even after your arrival, you did not look at any of these or study these so at least you would be familiar with the various constitutions of these republics?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in your particular case, fair to say, you only had to concern yourself with one particular republic which eventually became a state, and that was Bosnia and Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You knew -- you knew before coming in theatre that there -- there was a war going on, or conflict?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You termed it as a civil war as you understood it then and as you understand it today; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I wouldn't hang myself on any particular definition. Yes, conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Yeah, but when you think of the greater picture of Yugoslavia, now people are fighting inside, it's a civil war in a sense.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We can quarrel about the legal terminology of a civil war, but -- all right. And, of course, you must have been familiar that with the greater context of the conflict going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was also a conflict that had occurred or a war in the Republic of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And to a large extent, that conflict by the time you arrived had taken -- that is, the conflict with the Republic of Croatia, had taken a different turn in the sense that it was no longer continually being attacked by the former JNA or the JNA or whatever you want to call them?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it, I take it from all of these answers that you knew little, if any, of what would -- had been happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the time when the JNA was attacking the Republic of Croatia. And let me --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. And would it be fair to say that to what extent the JNA had been using -- had been operating within the territory of Bosnia- Herzegovina, you know, and using that as a staging ground to attack Croatia, I take it you had little or no knowledge of as well?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Some knowledge. Were you aware by any chance or did you ever become aware of what the reaction was of the Croat people in Bosnia- Herzegovina in relation to its government, that is the government of the Bosnia-Herzegovina and how it was reacting towards -- and how it was responding towards the JNA vis-a-vis using -- the JNA using BiH territory to attack Croatia? I know it's a long -- you understood what I meant?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian Community in Bosnia-Herzegovina established a defence council to protect their interests and resisted passively, at first, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were you aware by any chance of efforts that the Croatian -- the Croatians of Bosnia and Herzegovina pre-dating the community in a sense, any efforts they had made in sounding the -- the alarm, placing a clarion call as it will, to Izetbegovic and the government in Sarajevo to do something, to arm itself, to protect itself, to gear up for perhaps the winds of war blowing, you know, from north to south, you know? Were you aware of any efforts that the Croats in Bosnia had made in that fashion?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in detail, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. By the time that you arrived, by the time that you arrived, ECMM had been out of country or out of theatre for some period of time.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm not quite sure on the date, maybe you can help us out. When was it exactly that the ECMM returned to -- to the theatre? To Bosnia, that is.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: December 1992, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether it was beginning, middle or end of December?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you spoke of Mr. Lane as being sort of the hands-on and more or less the old-hand within the ECMM -- I guess it would be the coordinating centre that you were operating on. Do you know when he arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In December. Had he been there before the -- before that -- that gap?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So in essence, by the time you had arrived, he had in total of approximately one month in theatre. That was the total, the sum total, of his experience in Bosnia-Herzegovina as an ECMM monitor; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, though I can't be correct about his dates of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know, and I'm not going to hold you to this and if you don't know then say so, but do you know if he had served in any other capacity in -- in theatre which would then -- which at least would say he had some previous knowledge of what on earth was happening in Bosnia- Herzegovina before he became an ECMM monitor?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You don't know or no, he did not have any?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he had some experience in the Krajina --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the months before he entered Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to talk a little bit about the orientation that you received when you arrived, and as I understand it correctly, it was from January 2nd you arrive, and you leave on the 8th. So we're talking relatively five days of -- to be briefed.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, was this a formal briefing or was this somewhat of a -- sort of a casual briefing, people coming in and going out? Was there some sort of a structured briefing, as it were?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a structured briefing carried out in the hotel in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I take it there was like a little room or a conference room where people sat? Usually you get a little folder and maybe a pen and pad. Did you get -- was that provided?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slightly more -- slightly more advanced than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Slide show or --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. I guess the military loves these presentations with the computers. Well, the question is, I guess, in your briefing packet, can you describe to us, can you describe to us what exactly did it contain that would equip you in understanding who you were dealing with and what your purpose was? In brief, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The briefing focused principally on the front lines at the time as they would seem to be between the parties in conflict. They dealt with the issues, particularly where front lines were live, and we received relatively little information but sufficient for us to understand that the regions we were deploying to were on the whole stable, that is, within what we understood then to be the federation between the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. In particular, did they by any chance provide you with a list of the who's who in at least the very -- the region that you were going to be dealing with?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received that in Split when I deployed to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Well, before we get to Split, did they at least -- did -- was there any -- I don't want to say political, but sort of an orientation on how the government itself functioned? In other words, from the state and then on to the various communities or what have you. Did they have a flowchart, an organisational chart so you could say okay this is how politically it operates, and here is where the levels of power are. Was there any sort of orientation on that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't shown one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You were not shown one then and I take it when you got to Split and eventually got to -- got in theatre, would it be fair to say you weren't shown one there either?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ray Lane explained to me when I arrived what the layout was, who the principal personalities were that he was dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Again, you know, and I don't mean to be a stickler about this, I'm asking whether one was shown to you, because Lane is giving you an oral -- a verbal presentation, and I'm interested in whether one was down on paper that would -- at least we could check, not that I just -- well, actually, I do mistrust Lane. I don't know what he was saying to you. I don't know whether it's accurate or not, but was there one that had been compiled so as you would leave and the next person would come in, there is some sort of an organisational history, an institutional history, as it were, and as the situation changed and became -- because it was rather fluid, one could trace, for instance, how things were changing politically, structurally, legally, and what have you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, that is Ray and I, prepared those at the time. He was drafting them and over the weeks we prepared them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it we can find -- were those sent off as part of your reporting system?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not initially, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Lane was there for a total of one month. Did he by any chance give you an orientation on the government in Sarajevo, the state -- at the state level, who was who?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you know -- did you know who was -- did you know who was the number one person in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And -- and his -- and the title of his position was what?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, officially if you recall?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Leader of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Leader -- well, if ask you who the leader is -- what is the top person in the UK you're going to tell me --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He was the president?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know how this president -- how -- do you know below him how the structure worked?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In other words -- let me just -- let me just help you out here. If you look at the flowchart of -- because we're dealing with Europe, you may have a president, you may have a Prime Minister. Sometimes the Prime Minister is more -- has more powers than the president. It all depends on the country. In Greece, it's the Prime Minister and not the president. In France, it's the president and not the Prime Minister. Now, do you know below the president what the structure was, the political structure?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and the principal reason for that is because in the area in which we were operating to begin with, those authorities had little influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, when you arrived, you weren't -- were you aware of that and as a result you decided there was no need to -- to learn of how the system worked, or was that something that eventually you came to realise, well, Sarajevo has nothing to do or has no influence here, there's no need to worry about it? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Principally, the concern it start with was to observe what was happening rather than necessarily to understand all of the background.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it became apparent relatively quickly that the Bosnia- Herzegovina government's position in Sarajevo was isolated from the remainder of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Would it -- would it surprise you that first of all he was the president but he was the president of a Presidency? Would that surprise you to learn?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know how this Presidency worked?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, later on we're going to get to a document, but what is interesting in the document, and you'll have to trust me for the moment on it, is that Mr. Ganic is mentioned, and he's referred to in the ECMM documents by ambassadors as the vice-president of -- of Bosnia- Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would have used that terminology, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Now, would it surprise you, sir, would it surprise you to learn that at the time there was no such position in the structure, the political structure based on the constitution of a vice-president in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but again our concern was not with what was what people called themselves, referred themselves as or each other but what was actually taking place in theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. I understand that, but I guess what I'm -- the point that I'm trying to make is here you are in country, here you're trying to find out who the interlocutors are, and you're trying to figure out, you know, how you can possibly help in this rather chaotic situation, and you have ambassadors in the ECMM referring to someone who is a member of the Presidency, a mere member, and incidentally the Presidency worked -- Izetbegovic was the first among equals, that's all he was, but he's being referred to as the vice-president. In other words, giving him more power, at least the perception of power, due to him. Do you find that somewhat -- do you think possibly that -- that that might be a cause of concern? How is it that these people, that ECMM is there, ambassadors, not just you, but others much higher than you, don't even know the political structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina, yet they're jumping to conclusions?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can understand why the misuse of terminology might aggrieve some or cause confusion. For us, it was a question of reporting what was happening rather than any label attached to any particular person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And -- now, you had an opportunity to be in the presence of Mr. Ganic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I suspect if ambassadors are referring to -- ambassadors from ECMM are referring to him as -- in their documents, that is, as vice- president in person, would they have referred to him as well as Mr. Vice- president? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall us only referring to him as Mr. Ganic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did he ever represent himself to be vice-president?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course had he represented himself to be the vice-president and had ECMM relied on that, that, of course, would be rather troubling because in a sense he would be perpetrating a fraud; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suggest we will be talking to him because we felt he could deliver.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That wasn't my question now, was it? Let me ask you -- tell you again. If, in fact, Mr. Ganic was representing himself and leading everyone else on to believe that he was indeed the vice-president, the number two in the government, when in fact he was merely a member of the Presidency, that representation would be a fraud. He would be committing a fraud on the ECMM. It would be --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It would be a misrepresentation; right? And in one instance, and there's a document that I wanted to go through with you, it's very clear that he says at a meeting that he -- he's there to represent the Muslims as the representative of the Muslims. Is that how understood his position to be, as to be a member of the Presidency of the vice-president or the deputy or whatever you want to call him but there primarily for the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You know, whereas there was one instance I think when Mr. Boras was there, and he would be looked upon as someone for the Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And yesterday, there was a question, I believe it was by Ms. Alaburic, where she had -- she had asked you about Mr. Izetbegovic and you had, in fact, indicated that he was the representative of the Muslim people in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had become that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. All right. And so it would -- it -- if you, as ECMM, would view that, and quite naturally so, would it not also be -- be equal -- equally true and equally apparent, perhaps, to others such as the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina that Alija Izetbegovic was there first and foremost as a Muslim representative or the representative of the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really suggest how the Croatian Defence Council might have seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about the average Croat. Here you as an ECMM see him as the representative of the Muslim -- of the Muslims, okay? And that's fine, because I think that's how he projected himself. Would not -- would that not also equally apply to others than yourself like -- such as the Croats, the Croat counterparts?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croat counterparts were quite specific who they wished to deal with and who they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't ask who they wanted to deal with. I -- we're going to go step-by-step on this one. Okay?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Could you repeat the question then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The question is as follows: ECMM, and you being one of them, saw Mr. Izetbegovic as being the Muslim representative, just as Mate Boban being the representative for the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Radovan Karadzic for the Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite as straightforward as that because Mr. Izetbegovic would have liked it to be understood that he acted for a group of people living in a particular part of Bosnia and that included, in my experience, people likeMr. Boris, Colonel Siber, from a number of nations, so it wasn't quite as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, but of course what you're talk -- and I understand what he would have liked to have wished to legitimise his position in the sense, but needless to say even under those conditions he's wearing two hats, is he not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you would -- would you not expect at any negotiations that Izetbegovic would be at, he would be first and foremost looking after his people? I mean, he's not going to give away things that are going to be hurtful to his people; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you know whether -- I want to -- before we go on, just since we're on this topic and you mentioned what Mr. Izetbegovic would have wished, and I'm going to refer to a document, 1D 00814, and I'm going to -- this is from a book that has been used in this courtroom before, it's a compilation of a variety of documents including a speech by Lord Owen. I don't know if we have it on screen. It's a short passage I wish to read. It's on page 214 of this particular book, a speech by Lord Owen. This is at a ministerial level meeting of the steering committee of the international conference on the former Yugoslavia, 16 December 1992. And the passage I wish to read is on the third paragraph starting from the top of the page it says - of page 2, page 2 of the document, I have to apologise, we have these fancy new systems. Okay. If we look at the third paragraph, it says: "One of our concerns is that Bosnia and Herzegovina -- is that the Bosnian and Herzegovian Government is sadly increasingly becoming representative only of the Muslim population." Now, this is Lord Owen, 16 December, 1992, prior to your arrival. Now, if Mr. Owen, who was involved in these negotiations, has this perception from his dealings with Mr. Izetbegovic and from all his contacts and all his involvement which you would agree was at least at the negotiating level much higher than yours, it would seem, would it not, that Izetbegovic was indeed looking after the interests of his people more or less much -- at least much more than those of the others and was not really a representative of the government of BiH but of the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can understand that, though I'm not really qualified to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Then you could understand, could you not, and I mention this only because you make a reference, and the Prosecution has brought this up, I believe, but that there is a reference to this meeting at Citluk that took place, there was a statement that was issued, where -- where the Croats, the Croatian Community, Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina through their -- their representatives, had indicated that they no longer viewed Izetbegovic as the head of the state but, rather, as the head of the Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if we look at Mr. Owen's viewpoint in December, 1996, in this -- this Citluk -- the minutes from the meeting, and by -- and we can look at it very briefly. I'm trying to go through -- this one is on May 5, 1993. So it wasn't until about six months late that's right Croats finally came out and say that they don't view Mr. Izetbegovic -- and they view actually his Presidency as illegal. If we could look at document 1D 00817. And this would be on the fourth page under paragraph eight. I'll just read it while it's being pulled up on the screen to save time. "Presentation and legitimacy of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic taking position of the president of BiH Presidency is illegal. Croat people consider Mr. Izetbegovic only as the official representative of the Muslims in BiH. In the same way, BiH army may be legitimate only as the armed forces of Muslim people." In light of what we know from Mr. Owen's observations and in light of what you've already told us based on your experience or what you understood it would be that Mr. Izetbegovic was, in fact, the leader of the Muslim people, one could understand that back in May, in light of all the activities that were going on that the Croats would view Izetbegovic in those terms, especially in dealing with him at the negotiating table; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could express that view, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that view would be understandable, would it not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated in -- I believe in your testimony that you were not a student of the -- of HDZ or HVO -- of the HVO structure, and I -- I take it you stand by that.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And by that I take it that what you mean is when you -- just as you did not -- and were not provided with the structure at the government level, at the state level, the same could be said at the local level in the sense that you did not look at any particular legislation or any particular material that might be available that would allow you to understand how the HVO was structured; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course Mr. Lane, having been there before you, new some thingsobviously he had -- he had been briefed, but suffice it to say, at least when I read some of your statements, it would appear that your understanding was during this period Mr. Prlic was the Prime Minister; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it surprise you if I were to tell you that in fact he was not the Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, a label is a label. The situation was not quite as simple as that, but I'll take your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, did you -- did you understand how this community -- let me -- let me -- I'll ask it in a more open-ended fashion. How did you understand this community to function, that is, it included various municipalities, and how did the -- how were the municipalities structured, and what was their relationship with Mr. Boban and perhaps Mr. Prlic and anyone else within the system? What was your understanding of it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As was perhaps described yesterday, as representatives of a national group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But were you aware that there was a Presidency and Mate Boban was the president of a Presidency as opposed to just being the president? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if I were to ask you who were the members of the Presidency, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not officially, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would it surprise you to learn that primarily were -- the presidents of the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what the presidents of the municipalities, what sorts of powers they had at the local level, both over civilian life as well as over the military, if any?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We looked at it more in terms of influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that, but --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the ability to get things on or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we're going to get there, but you're going to ask that -- if you could answer my question.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen a document that lays out their responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever ask for a document and not receive one?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you ever ask for an explanation and not receive one?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say while you were working along with Lane and others, the fact of the matter was that other than your understanding of where you could look to for influence, for all intents and purposes, you were -- you lacked an appreciation of -- at least at the local level of how it operated and who was in charge?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think our communications were very effective, and if the people we had connections with felt that we were ill-advised or could have done it better, they had the opportunity to advise us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, that's the second time. I don't want to get -- I don't want to have to get into this too much because particularly Judge Trechsel doesn't like it, but if you could just answer my question. The answer is that you did not have an appreciation of the political leadership at the municipal level, and it would be fair to also say that you did not have an appreciation of what, if any, influence they may have had over the military at the local level?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you do make a reference at least at one point in time, I can find it, and it refers to General Petkovic, where in a sense he, at one time, is issuing a particular order over the phone and the local leader simply refuses; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And refuses because he felt he could.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well -- and in fact, General Petkovic tried and tried and eventually succeeded, but in fact there was a clear indication, at least at that level, the clear example where at least some folks at the local level had control over both civilian and military matters; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, one would think, one would think that at least -- oh, sorry. Sorry, sorry. I'm trying my best. I think I'm doing fairly well today. Now, one would think, one would think that at least after that sort of incident an effort would be made to figure out how this structure all works, but none was made; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not as simple as that. Again, it comes back to some fairly critical situations that needed some attention and resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our obligation was to do our best to reach satisfactory conditions to develop any kind of dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to back up a little bit. We talked a little bit about your orientation. Now I want to talk about, at least from the military structure. Were you by any chance, being a military man, of course, you might have been interested, but were you by any chance given any instructions on the military doctrine that existed prior to the break- up of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it you had not heard of what was known as the All Peoples Defence?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you -- were you explained at all about how the Territorial Defences operated within the All Peoples Defence?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only from, yes, a national Yugoslav approach to its own defence in preceding years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And -- well, could you explain -- do you recall what it was or would you like me to refresh your memory? Either way.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be helpful for you to refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Or not good. I'll do so. Would it be, as I understand it and we've heard it in court and we'll hear it again, you had the JNA, but also at the very local level you had what is known as Territorial Defences where, in the event Yugoslavia would be attacked from the outside, at the local level there was a stockpile of weapons, there was -- everybody was mobilised. There had been training, a 50-year indoctrination. This was taught in schools. So at the very local level, they would be able to organise themselves both politically and militarily, and from there you would have this Territorial Defence working in conjunction with the professional army, the JNA, to ward off any foreign aggressors. And this was both men and women, ages 16 to 60. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you've said it much better than I could have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, so -- would it surprise you to learn that this was done both at the republic level, that is various republics, but also then even way down to the grassroots level so that when the war broke out, when the civil war broke out, the communities were able at least to organise themselves based on -- they were already self-organised, but some may even have a stockpile of weapons from which to develop a Territorial Defence to defend themselves? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I mentioned that because I -- you make one reference. You muse to the fact that you could not understand why at times you had -- you and the ECMM had a hard time finding out how the armija was structured and who was at the top and who was going to -- who -- how it was structured and what have you, and you muse that perhaps it was because they had to form themselves overnight. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I can quote you if you wish, but basically that's what you say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm listening to the translation, but now I would like only to say there is a question of detail, but you mentioned that in the Yugoslav Peoples Army, all men and women from ages 16 to 60, they were trained and to be ready for a kind of war or other situations. I wonder if you took it from some sources which are really, I would say, contained in these figures of 16 and 60, because I'm not aware of that. Probably some of even the accused might -- might instruct you if you were correct on those numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Especially if we speak about also the women and men and the younger, I would say, children or boys of the age of 16. So I wonder if this -- I would say, this kind of statement could be either confirmed or denied. And I'm also taking the floor in order to give some respite for you and Mr. Beese because it was a long diatribe that we have heard. So thank you, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let me make sure that I'm clear. I'm talking about the Territorial Defence, the TO. Secondly, the All Peoples Defence was something that was taught at school. The age at the time, the military age, in case of an emergency was 16 to 60, and during the course of the proceedings we will be presenting evidence to establish that. Of course, I'm glad you brought it up. Make a note of it and make sure that I do establish that, and that's very important I'm glad you mention it because -- and as we see in all parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war, that is a critical date or critical figure, 16 to 60, because every man, at least, is viewed as a military combatant or capable military combatant, and so that's -- that's the importance of that. But thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we were talking, I believe, about a -- you make a reference that there were -- there was a -- you and others in the ECMM had a difficult time trying to figure out who was in charge or where did the powers lie with the armija, and you muse, and I quote: "Perhaps it was a consequence of having formed a citizens army at such a short notice." I mean, that was your understanding of it; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the possibilities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One of the possibilities. And of course not knowing that there was already -- well, maybe you knew and maybe you didn't give it much thought, that the Territorial Defence actually at the very local level presented itself as an opportunity for each community to self-organise; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Though some were evidently much more effective than others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And that would have been the same with the Croats as well?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you know when the armija was formed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We talked a little bit about the HDZ. We just barely mentioned it, but the SDA that was the political party for the Muslims, was it not, or the predominant political party for the Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And were you aware whether at any point in time they had a military wing?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, would it surprise you to learn that in fact at the very outset they did? In fact, they formed what was known as the Patriotic League and none other than Halilovic was one of the architects and masterminds behind it as he takes credit in his own book? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it if you weren't aware of it, perhaps Mr. Lane wasn't aware of it either since he didn't brief you on it. He might not have been aware of it.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. In that particular region that you were serving in your area of responsibility, there was some sort of military -- military industry at some point in time, was there not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you know where exactly it was located?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Heliodrom south of Mostar, principally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that was for the -- I believe it was for the -- if my memory serves me correctly, for helicopters or what have you, but what about in the Travnik area, that area up there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were munitions factories, I believe, across Bosnia- Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And was there any munitions factory around there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did you as a military man ever try to find out what exactly at least in your neck of the woods, your area of spot, what exactly, if any, munitions were being manufactured, which might, of course, be a bone of contention or -- or a prize to capture by one side or the other?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Different -- different communities, that is different towns had factories that produced component parts. Therefore, it would have been of interest to have more than one to assemble a particular weapon or munition, perhaps, but I don't have specific details, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you never visited these -- any of these factories?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could -- I want to talk a little bit about the assessment, the assessment process, before we move on a little bit, and I'm going to recap, because this was mentioned a while -- when you first testified, and some of us may have forgotten it. As I understand it, there was the ECMM headquarters in Zagreb; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then there was a regional centre, or there were regional centres, one being in Zenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then, of course, there were coordinating centres, one of them being in Grude or --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It was called the Grude, but actually you folks were situated in Siroki Brijeg; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What is the distance between Siroki Brijeg and Grude, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 45 minutes drive. I can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And would it be fair to say during that period of time the road was rather clear? You could travel that road, Siroki Brijeg to Grude?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And when you -- when you got there in country, as I understand it, Grude is where Mate Boban was located.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Incidentally, when you first got into the country, in theatre, I mean, my experience, having worked in these sort of international missions, is that one of the first things you do is make up some printing cards, calling cards, and then you arrange to go and see all the local officials to let them know, you know, that you arrived, you know, become acquainted and so on and so forth. Did Mr. Lane do that with you? In other words, take you on the rounds in somewhat of a structured way, so at least from the very beginning you would know who's who?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was introduced to number of civic leaders in communities across Southern Herzegovina, which was principally my area to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was this in some sort of a structured area, structured format so you say, Okay, today we're going to meet the leaders of the HVO. Tomorrow we're going to meet the leaders of the, you know, the Muslim leaders or -- how was this done?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you, in fact, did meet Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You did not. Well, you did -- you did participate at least in a meeting in which he was -- he was present, and that would have been, I believe, if my memory serves me correct, May 8th, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that was the very first time that you met Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And from reading your testimony and other documents, it would appear, it would appear that it was at that particular moment, upon seeing the dynamics at that meeting, that you realised that Mate Boban was the most important person or the most powerful person within the Croatian Community; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So -- in other words, you knew that prior to -- prior to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And would it be fair to say, then, that if you had a particular problem that you wanted resolved, that's the person that you would go to? Maybe not first, but ultimately -- or perhaps even first if it was urgent; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would generally have approached Mate Boban through the regional centre and not directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. In other words, you would have somebody much higher than you approach him?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But that wasn't the case with Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic was happy to see us on many occasions. If he felt it was inappropriate he would offer us an alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you suggesting that Mate Boban was not happy to see you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But since you did mention Mr. Prlic and happiness at seeing you, one would say, at least from I read, was that here was a gentleman that was -- his door was always open to the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In other words, he was accessible; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And whether you believed him or didn't believe him, he always indicated his willingness to assist?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I don't want to get ahead of myself, but this point was touched upon yesterday with the abduction of the Serbs. I believe the date was February 6, 1993. There was a round made to the various individuals, including Mr. Prlic and Mr. Boban, and as far as I understand, it was -- it was mentioned by you that you thought that any -- that the representation that they had made that they would conduct an investigation were hollow words. Do you recall saying something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it turns out that after what we saw yesterday from the -- from the lawyer, from counsel for Mr. Coric and then Mr. Coric as well at some point, it would appear that perhaps you had jumped the gun on that one, at least, that they were not hollow words, that efforts were made to investigate. Perhaps not to your satisfaction and of course not to your knowledge, but would it be fair to say that at least on that instance, efforts were made?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was done. I can't say how much effort was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, as a military man having been in theatre where there's action, you do appreciate the fact that it's -- they're working under abnormal circumstances, were they not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And by your own admission, you had indicated that on both sides, on both sides there were elements that -- I don't want to use extreme because that's a different issue, but there were elements that simply were uncontrollable; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when you're dealing with those sorts of uncontrollable elements, one has to be rather careful for their own safety, their own life; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was that the people we're talking of in the government of the HVO had the control and influence to be able to resolve these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that was your understanding. We saw efforts being made, and we saw the ultimate report. Obviously it took longer than you or anybody else would have wished, but you cannot sit here with any degree of certainty and say that under those circumstances, one did not have to at least tread lightly on certain matters irrespective of nationality or ethnicity involved, because there were a lot of dangerous people, dangerous and crazy people running around?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before we get -- I just want to go back now to what we were talking about. We -- the structure. As I understood you, the regional centre would assess and analyse whatever information they received from the coordinating centres; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the coordinating centres would prepare a daily report based on what they had learned from the teams; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it would be then the regional centres that would type up a report and then send it to the headquarters; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then from the headquarters the ECMM --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. I thought I was going very slow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And -- and so it would be the -- the regional centres would prepare these reports, send them to the headquarters -- to the headquarter, and from the headquarter another report would be compiled, and that would be to the ambassadors of the ECMM countries, including Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- and so we could safely say that at least the end product that was ultimately reached by -- or obtained from ECMM started at the very grassroot level, from the team approach; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So when Mr. Owen would look at something or Mr. Vance would look at something from the ECMM, it would be based on what was seen, observed, heard, analysed, and then compiled at the team level first, and it would move up the chain; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm being slow to answer only to assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, here's what I'm interested in: I mean, you've talked about assessment and analysis, but you didn't really tell us how was this information assessed and analysed. Who were these people? What were their training? What was the protocol? I've been thinking about this, reading it, thinking, you know. And I guess here is a series of questions for which -- for you to ponder on and perhaps give us a lengthy explanation: Was there a set-up methodology, you know, a protocol? What sort of criteria was used? Was there any quality control, any double-checking? Was there any -- when the final assessment and analysis was performed, was it done on a consensual basis? Was there a consensus reached, or was it by one individual making that assessment, final assessment and analysis based on the information that he had received, keeping in mind, at least from what I understand from you, that that person would have been sitting somewhere in an office typing a report from data as opposed to sensing, feeling, seeing, hearing, or any empirical efforts? And my -- and finally, what about dissenting opinions? Were any dissenting opinions ever put in what happened to them if there were dissenting opinions so could you please tell us from your understanding, and I mention that because - and I think you're qualified to testify because you worked in the team at a coordinating centre and at a regional centre.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So could you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting at the grassroot level, each team or a team would normally have two monitors. The two monitors would discuss what they had seen and heard during the day and report that to the head of the coordination centre. That in itself is not normally a complicated process. The head of the coordinating centre would use a standard format for reporting issued by the ECMM covering a number of headers such as any economic issues, social issues, military issues, with space at the bottom for a summary. The head of coordinating center, in my experience, discussed his analysis with other senior monitors before submitting it. In the regional centre, in my experience, the reports coming in from the field would come in any time between 6.00 in the evening and 10.00 in the evening, and the process during the busy periods of putting those together would continue until about midnight when there was discussion between usually two to three senior members of the mission on the analysis. In my case whilst in the regional centre, it would have been two of three people who discussed the report before its submission. The head of the regional centre, in my experience, Ambassador Jean-Pierre Thebault, myself as deputy head of regional centre, and Mr. Remi Landry as chief operations officer for the regional centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that being said, it would appear that -- at least I can conclude that consensus was tried to be -- was reached before the final report went from the regional centre to the headquarters; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that would have been based on a discussion of data that was provided to those analysts, if you will, who had not seen or heard anything but were merely reading a report.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was any doubt there would be discussion, if possible, with the coordination centre submitting its reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you say if there was any doubt, does that mean that they would call you up?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You would call them. Well, how would you -- well, how would you know that there was doubt? How would you know when to call?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: For much of the period, the events that occurred were so significant that the focus given them was total, and if -- if there was conflict in one particular area, it would not have been a surprise to hear there was conflict necessarily. The difficulty was understanding why it was taking place then, there, and what that might mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stop. It's time for the break. It's a quarter to 4.00. We'll resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we recommence would it be convenient to indicate to us generally how much more time remains for cross-examination for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thanks to the registrar's hard work, whom I would like to thank, I'd like to tell you that you've used 4 hours and 23 minutes and we said yet that you would be having 8 hours. So theoretically you have 3 hours, 40 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we might need some more time, Your Honour. Not much, but hopefully that's not a fixed period. Keep in mind that we're having to go in and out of open court and what have you, so ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I might just be allowed to add two words to what counsel said. You did tell us 8 hours yesterday, that's quite true, but before that there was mention of two and a half days. So when we divided up the time among the Defence teams, we counted on having 10 hours. So that's where the problem arises. According to the Prosecutor's schedule, it seems that it was -- they planned to begin with a new witness tomorrow after half time, after the first half of the day. So I'd like to join in what my colleagues said. If we could be allowed two more hours tomorrow morning, because we're the last, Praljak and myself, and we have quite a lot of questions to ask. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as I'm concerned, I don't see any difficulty with that if the cross-examination is using the time properly, but I'd like to mention that Mr. Karnavas asked the witness questions about the -- how reporting was done and so on and so forth. Now, that's an interesting topic generally, but one question and one answer would suffice, but you spent quite a number of minutes belabouring the point. So that's where you use your time. Although it is all useful, we must justify the use of time. So on the question of whether you're going to be able to use tomorrow, that will depend on the Prosecution. Mr. Mundis, you were on your feet because the witness envisaged for tomorrow, can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, for this opportunity. Very briefly, the fact of the matter is if the Prosecution indicates that there are two witnesses on for a given day, as would be the case perhaps with respect to tomorrow's schedule, that does not necessarily mean that it's split in half, 50/50, in terms of the two witnesses that are scheduled to appear. We would also re-emphasise, from the Prosecution perspective, the point Your Honour, the Presiding Judge, just made with respect to the relevance. We have take and he decision not to object to a number of irrelevant or what we would object to as irrelevant questions for the simple reason that the Defence, as professionals, know the amount of time they have, and we don't also want to be in a position of the Defence saying, Well, if it weren't for the objections of the Prosecution, we would have finished and we don't want to eat up a lot of time in terms of objections. They know how much time they have. They know the relevant of the questions in the line of questioning they want to put to the witness, and it's up to the Defence to organise their work accordingly. Similarly, if one of the Defence teams thinks that they need more time, they can certainly address that with the cross-examining party in terms of organising their work. So our position would be, as Your Honour indicated, the Prosecution used about five and a half hours with this witness on direct, eight hours is certainly more than the Prosecution used, and to expand that to 10 hours is not the best use of the Trial Chamber's time given the fact that some of these questions are not necessarily relevant to the issues at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But as far as your witness is concerned, the one that you're going to call tomorrow, how much time will you need for the examination-in-chief of tomorrow's witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may assist my colleague. In the chart, they indicated 2.5 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two and a half hours. So since it's a witness who was a victim, the Defence will have two and a half hours as well, which means five hours for that next witness, which means that we must begin the examination of that witness tomorrow, and that in turn means that we have another hour and a half until the next break. After the break we're going to have another one hour, roughly, so that leaves two and a half hours. Then tomorrow almost three hours for the Defence. So roughly speaking, the Defence will have another three hours tomorrow, plus two and a half hours today, which makes it roughly five hours or, rather, between five and five and a half hours. So I think that you will be able to finish off within that time, so that after the second break tomorrow we can start off with the next witness. Having said that, please continue, Counsel Karnavas, but I would like to emphasise once again, try and get to the essential points. We are professional Judges. We understand your line of questioning. We, too, have many questions to ask the witness, but we are letting you ask yours, and usually the Judges have half an hour of questions.
