utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will endeavour to be better. I'm going to go out of sequence at this point because you raised the point that perhaps I took too much time in talking about the reporting process, one that we believe is important because of all the documents that the Prosecution wishes to introduce as if that they are true, accurate, and complete because they have the seal of approval of the ECMM, an organisation which the Prosecution believes should be trusted completely, utterly, and faithfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, you were -- at some point you became aware of what is known as the ultimatum of January 15th; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday, and we're going to go into this more in depth, but you told us yesterday that you, in fact, never saw this ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so -- but nonetheless, you understood that there was an ultimatum and accordingly acted on it.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, here's where I have to lay some background before I get to the documents. As I understand it, when you testified and what I say in other written form, on January 15th, just by chance, you are visiting the -- the head of the armija in Mostar, Mr. Pasalic; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was seeing the brigade commander, which was not Mr. Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. The brigade commander. And it was at -- and you were with Mr. Lane. This is on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at some point -- and that -- it was at that point in time when they had indicated that there was some sort of an ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Must be clear here. I wasn't with Mr. Lane on the first day when he went. I went the second day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So Mr. Lane went on his own?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you know whether it was afternoon or morning?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But nonetheless as I understand it, that particular evening there was a meeting at the regional centre and he went up to Split.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But when he went up to Split, he went up there armed with information that was given to him by the Muslim commander with respect to some sort of an ultimatum; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But as I understand your testimony, Mr. Lane spoke to you about this when he came back from the meeting and -- and in fact, told you words to the fact that -- not to expect too much cooperation or expect too much from the Muslim army at this point in time because they seemed somewhat agitated.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the following day, as I understand it, you were summoned or called to meet with these individuals, to meet with the armija, the Muslim commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You had only been in country for about eight days, and it was at that meeting that you saw Mr. Arif Pasalic, and I believe he was in an alcoholic haze of some sort, and it was at that point that his deputy read out a six-page document; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Mr. Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not Mr. Pasalic, his aide?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Pasalic was not present. I was meeting with a brigade commander. He did appear to be worse for wear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it was at that point that you were briefed about this so- called ultimatum and subsequently to the briefing, you contacted Mr. Lane; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you were summoned by Mr. Lane to come to Split to give some sort of a briefing to them?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you were in Mostar at the time, correct, when you got this briefing?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which side of the river were you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: West bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that's where the headquarters of the army of BiH were located?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Where was Mr. Prlic's office at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the west bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. How far would you say by car driving or even by walking, how long, how far of a distance was it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten minutes or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, upon hearing this information, recognising that it's rather alarming in a sense, so alarming that you contact Mr. Lane in -- in Split, you did not, in fact, make any efforts, you or the individual that was with you, to go and speak with Mr. Prlic or somebody else, anybody, to perhaps see whether indeed this ultimatum was true, accurate, and complete, you know, what was the nature of it, at least to have some information from the other side; right? No efforts were made.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Effort at that time would not have necessarily been the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's not the question that I'm posing. We're going to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You made no effort; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now I'm going to have to go a little faster.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So -- and to get ahead of myself based on what you just indicated to me, it seems that you were jumping the gun. You believed what you heard and, therefore, there was no need to talk to any Croat. Hell, Croats were going to lie to you. You might as well just believe what you heard and just go straight up to Split; right? I mean, that's what it appears.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Then please explain to you and explain to the Judges here why you didn't take -- make any efforts whatsoever, by your own admission, to at least hear the other side of the story to find out whether this ultimatum was true, what was the content of it, and so on and so forth. Please explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had not, at that stage, met Mr. Prlic. I was not fully briefed on the chain of command that I should apply to. We had barely met the armija people in Mostar. It was appropriate for me to pass it back to people who had more experience, more understanding, and could address it at the correct level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But if this was, in fact, such an emergency, okay, one would think that you would want to get all your facts correctly, not just you but ECMM. Did you by any chance ask Lane who might be the Croat counterpart, an interlocutory -- an interlocutor that you could meet and at least get some sort of a briefing with?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: By regarding it to Ray Lane, he report it had to the ambassador, and between them they had the choice as to what to do about it, and they ultimately decided, determined, to go to Mostar to speak with Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when they got to -- when they got to Mostar was what date?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: A few days later. So obviously the ultimatum was not so imminent that it required ECMM to act immediately. Because if you're waiting two or three days and it's an imagine, it's not really an imagine, is it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an important issue, not an emergency, but the deadline for the ultimatum was the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But needless to say, before heading up to -- when you went up to Split, the purpose for you being summoned, because that wasn't by your own decision, but the purpose was for you to give a briefing on what you had heard; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it would appear, at least from my point of view -- I'm trying to slow down but I'm pressed for time. There's no way I can cover everything. It appears to me that the higher-ups don't care what the other side has to say. They don't want to have the facts. They just want to hear from the one side. Might that be the case?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you of course never suggested well, maybe we should at least look at this ultimatum and see what it might say; right? You never asked that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall quite what my thought processes were then, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you draw a conclusion at some point that when the ambassador finally comes down and has a meeting with Mr. Prlic, you're not present but you're told by Mr. Lane that harsh words were spoken and in a sense, Mr. Prlic was instructed in no uncertain terms not to act on the -- on the ultimatum; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. You weren't present but that's what you were told. Hearsay, we call that here in this courtroom; right? You weren't there; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I mean, you might believe Lane but we have no reason to. But that's what you were told?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's what you recount?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you muse at some point, you speculate that perhaps the -- Mr. Prlic or others, Mate Boban, whoever, acted and did not go forward with the implementation of this -- of this so-called ultimatum based on the intervention of ECMM. And I can reference -- I can --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You draw that conclusion; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You, on -- now, it would be fair to say, would it not, and I'm not being critical so don't take this in any negative fashion, but obviously given where you were at in the totem pole, which is way down at the bottom, you were not privy to any papers or negotiations or discussions that were being held at a higher level.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you didn't see any exchanges of documents between the parties?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, first, since we're on this topic, and let's look at a document, and it's P 01215. This is a document that was generated by the ECMM signed by Mr. Beaussou, dated January 19, 1993, subject: Relations between Croat and Muslims visit to Mostar. Have you seen this document, sir? Is it on our screen? Have you seen this document, sir, before?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see all of it, but -- but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the first page just to see if you recognise it as a document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can everybody see it, because I can't see it on my screen? Do you have an extra copy here? This is part of the problem with -- here we go. We have an extra copy for the ELMO. If I could have the kind assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could look at the first page, it says the persons that were there, Mr. Jadranko Prlic -- okay. We have it on the screen. I don't know which one we want to look at. I have my own. All right. It says who attended, Mr. Prlic, Mr. Pasalic, Petkovic. And if we look at the second page of this document, okay -- well, first -- I apologise. Let's stick with the first page, because obviously I want you to look at it a little bit. Clearly we're talking about this particular incident, this particular period of time; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if we look into -- and if we look at the -- at the second page, it says here on paragraph B, I guess, it would be 3 (B): "After some misunderstandings in an exchange of letters, copies attached between government of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Prlic, and the Presidency of BiH, it is requested by Mr. Prlic to organise a meeting between Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban as soon as possible in Split. Such a meeting seems inasmuch necessary that there is really room for many clarifications, particularly in the period of uncertainty created by the new Geneva prospects." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go through this document and if you look at it, you won't see anything in this document about any harsh words being spoken to Mr. Prlic such as, Be careful because ECMM will do such-and-such. Nothing of the sort, but, rather, it seems that was a meeting, views were exchanged, there was a misunderstanding which we'll get to with the letters, and -- and the parties now are trying to clarify. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of this document back then?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That might be helpful, would it not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And I guess I'm asking you -- I was asked to put -- to point out that Mr. Petkovic, chief of -- if we look at the persons on the first page under 1, it says, "Mr. Petkovic, Chief of Staff, HVO, who stepped into our meeting, Mr. Pasalic, without formal notice." We can deal with this at some other point. Needless to say, what we have an account by none other than Mr. Beaussou as to what happened; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, before I talk about -- perhaps it might be a good idea now to look at the documents where he talks about the exchanging of information. If we could look at P 01267. Okay. Now, have you seen this document by any chance? This is a document -- it's a letter to Mr. Prlic from Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And just to make sure that we're talking about the right period, it says here: "The problems that have recently arisen among the members of BH army and HVO are not small, but they are not unsolvable as well." And it goes on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, does this document have a date? We do not see it and you have not mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Precisely. I'm going refer to another document that would at least clue us into the date of this letter. If we could look at document 1D 00818. And all I can tell you, Your Honour, is at the very top it says "ECMM Danish delegation." This is what I have at the time. But if we could look at this other document, this is 1D 00818, this is an agenda from minutes of a meeting that took place, and if we look at the agenda, it says "Analysis of Mr. Izetbegovic's letter. Item 1: On 17 January, 1993, the president of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, sent an invitation to Jadranko Prlic wherein he proposed talks in Sarajevo related to all contentious questions. The invitation came after an agreement reached by telephone that Izetbegovic's delegation should come to Mostar as soon as possible." From the top, we can see that this was generated on the 18th of January, 1993. I don't want to go in to this -- through the entire document, because the Court and the Judges can read it at some point and we're going to be introducing it, but were you aware that -- were you aware that this was happening?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And on page 2, we see after the analysis of Mr. Izetbegovic's invitation, the HVO HDZ decided unanimously to send the following response. That's on page 2 of this document. Following the telephone conversation of 16 January, 1995. So it would appear that on 16 January, prior to any intervention from ECMM, there is a conversation between Mr. Prlic and Mr. Izetbegovic. "We were in expectation of the announced arrival of your delegation to Mostar." Obviously Mr. Izetbegovic made some promises. "Having in mind the existence of a new situation in some municipalities of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna (Gornji Vakuf, Jablanica, Mostar and others) and your proposal to change the venue for the meeting - under the existing circumstances, unfortunately we cannot but interpret it as another of your numerous inconsistencies and undetermined political moves." And it goes on. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, had you been in theatre and had you spoken to the who's who in the Croatian Community, you would have heard, as undoubtedly you did, that one of the complaints that they had with Mr. Izetbegovic was that he often changed his mind, and he was rather inconsistent in keeping promises; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, you allude to that fact in one of the documents that parties would sign up to agreements that never really intended to comply with; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that would go for the Muslims as well, would it not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that would go not just for military agreements or agreements for cease-fire but also for peace agreements as well, would it not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, when you made that comment, it was in reference to negotiations that were ongoing with respect to solving the difference -- the differences between the Muslims and the Croats at a very high level, the Vance-Owen Peace Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, from here, assuming that the minutes were correct, these minutes from 18 January, and of course they were prepared well in advance of -- of these proceedings, it would appear that almost immediately there was some sort of communication to try to resolve this misunderstanding that the occurred whereby the Croats had begun to initiate what they believed was an agreement that had been reached at very high levels with the assistance of the International Community; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to move to another document that might help us out and here is perhaps this might -- finally we'll get to the area that Mr. President was mildly commenting on that perhaps I dwelled too much on, the fact of the reporting process, but this goes to why we must look at the documents in rather a very careful fashion and not just accept them. If I could make -- if I could refer you to a document, P 01303. I trust it's already in the system. And if we look at this, if we look at this document, it's dated - - it's dated 25 January, 1993. Do you see that, sir? And is this sort of a document that you might recognise?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we flip to the second page, we will see that it says, "Regards Beaussou," and this is a document -- well, why don't you tell us from where to where is this statement going?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we go back to the top, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to the first page, please, it says, "From HRC Split" that would be the regional centre Split; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To headquarters Zagreb; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the second page at the very top, number 4, he says, "I went to this meeting to Mostar, especially to have a private interview with Mr. Prlic, president of the government in the HVO, in order to express our deep concern. He said he understood the problem and shared our concern. As a matter of act," probably fact, "order was given on Saturday to Colonel Siljeg to stop immediately any attack and obey the orders." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And -- now, based on this, if we look at the next document, P 01319, first if we look at the first page, perhaps we can dwell on it a little bit just at the very top to see what is it. It says "ECMM operations section," and then you see a list of distribution. And towards the middle of the page, it says "Daily monitoring activity, 25 January 1993." Who prepared this report, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm trying to save time, Your Honours. I apologise, but I feel like I'm drowning, given the time limitations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can we look at this? Now, you see the distribution; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it would appear that it's going to the capitals or it's going to the foreign ministries of those who are participating in this ECMM process.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the document I'm looking at, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. Is this P 1309? P 01309. If we could put this on the ELMO to save time. We could take off whatever is on there. So if we could look at that. And do you recognise this sort of a document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what is -- what is this document? Where does it come from? How is it generated?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see at the moment where it's from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stop. This document is under seal. We have to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could look at 1D 00819. And while this is being looked -- we're getting it up, this is an HVO staff and BH army staff document. It's an order dated 20 January 1993. If we look at the last page, it has Mr. Petkovic -- General Petkovic's signature or name to it with a -- which is signed and stamped along with Arif Pasalic's. And it would seem that if we could look at this, is this not, sir -- have you seen this by any chance?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall, I'm afraid, without seeing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could look at the rest of -- I don't know how to work this thing. I could give you a private copy if you want to flip through. It might help while we still have this on. We don't need this on the ELMO. If you just -- if we could look at the rest of the document slowly. But this is an order, is it not? At least it purports to be.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it's dated on the 20th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it appears that an order has already been issued with respect to the situation, sir, that's ongoing in Gornji Vakuf; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So if we look at this now in conjunction with the previous two documents, it's quite clear that the last -- the last document that we looked at, the one that came from Zagreb and that was distributed outwards is rather misleading, because here we have an order for the 20th of January, and if you look at the first document that we looked at for Mr. Beaussou, clearly it would appear now that his English is rather good, because he says, "Order was given on Saturday." He's looking backwards. So an order was given. But nowhere in the first document does he say that Prlic gave the order. Here is an order signed by Petkovic and Pasalic; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presumably General Petkovic would have received instructions from higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, having said that, you had indicated to us before that you had not looked at and was not familiar with and was not a student of the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know who was the Supreme Commander for -- for the Croat -- for the HVO? The Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with use of that terminology, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would it surprise you if I were to tell you that there's actually legislation in place at that time, while you were there, that would give you that precise answer, and if fact, there was legislation that delineates rather quite clearly where the powers lie, who is responsible for what? Would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be surprised, if we relied on those structures, that there would have been loss of life that there later was. So I can't rely upon a structure described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I know you can't rely on it, but I guess what I'm trying to do is get you to admit that you were in total ignorance of it and the ignorance derives from your lack of interest or appreciation or need to understand what the actual political structure was, because it would seem to me, and correct me if I'm wrong, if I need to solve a problem, I need to know exactly who to go to, and that structure might give me the opportunity to know exactly who I need to address. Would you -- would that --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of February, at the very time we were talking peace with seep your officials in Mostar, Jablanica was shelled, Ahmici was attacked, and so forth. It's quite difficult in those circumstances to understand who is who, who is really in charge, and actually what the agenda is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If I could look at -- I want show you another couple of documents. If I can show you now, relative to these events because since you're here I think it might be interesting to look at, and we -- we would need to look at both the Croatian and -- do we have the Croatian one as well? 1D 00820 is a document. It's an unofficial translation. I do have the original or a copy of the original -- a copy of the original that I could put on the ELMO to show so we have it at least on the record. And keeping in mind that you and I can't read that, but I want to show the condition that we have it in, which would account for why we say that there is an illegible text to it. Yeah. And incidentally, just to -- I'm reminded with the excitement of it all, Ahmici, there was nothing in Ahmici in -- as you recall -- as you describing it in February but, rather, it was much later, in April 19 -- April 16, 1993. But in any event --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise for the inaccuracy, but the relevancy still stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to get to that. We're going to get to that. And I would agree with you the situation was a tinder box especially around January 15th, being correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so keeping in mind keeping in mind it is a tinder box and the situation is explosive. One would understand for instance if a communication is relayed from Geneva that there is, in fact, an agreement that you would want to at least prevent the situation from getting out of control because Gornji Vakuf had already started prior to the 15th or the 13th, there was some clashes and what have you, you would expect, would you not, for there to be some -- some initiative to be taken such as, perhaps, the ultimatum that was -- that we call it whereby, in some areas, ABiH troops are asked to subordinate themselves to the HVO and vice versa in other areas. In other words, HVO to subordinate themselves to armija. That's a solution that in order to deal with that explosive tinder box situation; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, given that you would understand my concern hearing that there was an ultimatum that might give rise to conflict and that therefore I should treat it very seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. And of course at that time, you were operating without the understanding and knowledge and appreciation that at least at a much higher negotiating level, there was a belief and understanding that an agreement had been reached between the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: But perhaps it wasn't happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that. What I'm trying to get at is this: Everybody is operating with a little bit of information, not all of it; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why we pass the information up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Beese, let me go back. I'll eat up some of my time on this one. You jumped the gun. You think it's necessary, you and Lane, you go up to Split and then Mr. Beaussou gets involved. What I'm suggesting also is that ultimatum that we call it was based on a belief that an agreement had been reached by the two sides that Izetbegovic had indeed agreed and for at least a change would stick by his word and that there was an initiative taken by the HVO because the Gornji Vakuf issue had started two or three days earlier and it appeared that it was going to get out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. This question is compound. There are a number of assertions in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For instance, I would like to hear what the assertion is. Which assertion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: "You jumped the gun." "You think it's necessary." "You and Lane you go up" -- there's a number of components in here. "Izetbegovic had indeed agreed and at least for a change would stick by his word."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I have to confess that I find it difficult to follow you, to follow your line of questioning. What do you want to establish? Could you ask a more synthetic question that would shed some light for the Judges on an element that you deem important. That has to be your objective, because if we are confused, if we are lost, then all your efforts are in vain. So could you please try to be more synthetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise for being rather convoluted. Let me go step-by-step.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, the situation in Gornji Vakuf had begun, or conflicts had begun as early as January 16th; is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thereabouts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Could it be even earlier?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So there was an ongoing crisis or an ongoing situation that was potentially going to become out of control by January 15th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suggest it began earlier in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I know what you suggest, but nonetheless, at this period of time it was -- the situation could have gotten out of control; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's suppose that one is of the understanding that an agreement has indeed been reached and Izetbegovic has indeed agreed to or what was being proposed in Geneva. Would it not be reasonable to act immediately on that in light of what you already told us of the situation, in order to prevent further precipitation of a conflict or to contain the conflict?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but one side giving instructions to the army of another is not likely to be taken well unless there is sound preparation for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, whether it's going to be taken well or not, that's a different issue. The first issue is one might want to act immediately; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say it's not going to be taken lightly, I take it the same could be said about the Croats that had to subordinate themselves to the Muslim army. They weren't going to like it either; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a question of liking it. It's a question of whether the planning and preparation makes it possible for a peaceful or cooperative endeavour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But would you expect that if the Muslims felt that way, the Croats who also had to subordinate themselves to the Muslims would equally feel that way as well; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a degree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So -- all right. So -- now if we could go back to this document. It's signed by Mr. Boban. At least that's what it appears at the bottom in the original. And this is dated January 20th. It says: "In reference to your decision," and it makes reference to a decision, "and after the discussion with the co-chairmen of the Geneva conference of Bosnia Herzegovina, Mr. Vance and Lord Owen, I am ordering you to convene a special meeting of the HVO HDZ -- HZ HB," I'm sorry, "during the day and change item 5 in a way to set a deadline for implementation of the decision," so on and so forth, we can't read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry to go back a little step because I simply do not understand. You said -- or you asked the witness to say what Muslims would feel --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- that had to subordinate themselves, that Croats that had to subordinate themselves to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's line -- now, that was a hypothetical or what facts do you exactly refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we have to look at the so-called ultimatum, which the gentleman never looked at. If you look at the ultimatum, Your Honour, you'll see that it's not a one-way street in implementing this -- what -- what was believed to have been reached as an agreement was that in some areas, those would be controlled, for instance, by the Croats, in order to have some kind of an organised military operation going because you had still the Serbs that you had to worry about, the Muslim army would subordinate itself to the -- to the Croatian. Vice versa in areas which were under control of the Muslims, and you had HVO operating, the hope officer -- the HVO would have to subordinate itself. We will get to that document at some point. But since the gentleman hasn't looked at it, never looked at it, never saw it, I'm trying to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- now, if we could go to the next document, because it might help us, it might help us, it might help us to understand what -- what -- the missing text. The missing text -- if we could look at 1D 00821. And in this decision -- this is dated January 20, 1993. So it appears, as was instructed, as was ordered, a special session was convened and a decision was taken. We can look at the preamble which makes reference to what we see above, and then it says the decision: "To change item 5 of the decision number 01-1-32/93 dated 15 January 1993, setting up a deadline for the implementation of that decision." And then it goes on to say in number 2 that: "Instead of the earlier deadline for subordination of units of army BiH, the command of the HVO General Staff in provinces 3, 8 and 10; and subordinating the HVO units to the army of BiH Command in provinces 1, 5 and 9" - Judge Trechsel, the answer to your question, "which was in five days, a new deadline is defined, and that is the end of the continued Geneva talks." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of this at the time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so one might conclude that at least when looking at all of these other documents, that your account is not quite as accurate when you say or when you speculate that in fact it was Mr. Beaussou's conversation or stern talking to Mr. Prlic as was -- as was related to but Mr. Lane that precipitated the events in calming the ultimatum and not going forward but rather there were letters of exchanges between Izetbegovic and Mr. Prlic, there was a decision, there were instructions by Mr. Boban based on his conversation with Lord Owen and Mr. Vance, and as a consequence that's how it was really resolved. Would it not appear so, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think my comments state that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. Would it not appear so, sir? Just answer my question. You can answer whatever question you want to answer.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The field of discussion and the documents made available to me are not known to me. They represent a degree of discussion which we would applaud now and then, but one's concern at the time was whether it was going to be successful or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, sir, but right now, you're testifying in this court, and you're trying to put my client in prison for the rest of his life with your testimony. So that's why, right now, what I'm showing is the rest of the story.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only comment on what I've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But it would appear that at the time that you wrote your - - that you -- you observed these events and later on wrote about them, you do not have -- you didn't have the benefit of all this information nor was it provided to you, was it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have an enormous amount of information. I wasn't commenting on the information I didn't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, the information that I'm giving -- showing you today shows a rather different picture than the one you have concluded.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Now, I'm going -- I've used already about two hours and 15 minutes. I'm going to speed up so I'm going to jump around a little bit, but needless to say, at one point in time, you relay an incident where you're asked by the government in Sarajevo, you and Mr. Andersen, I believe, to go to Geneva to give a briefing; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked to go so that, if questioned, I could give my view on facts as to whether they were correct or incorrect to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And you were invited to go there by Mr. Ganic, I take it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look at the documents, Mr. Ganic is referred to by Mr. Andersen as the vice-president of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So you go up there, and at some point you have and opportunity to meet with Lord Owen; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Lord Owen is a rather, you know, seasoned politician; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He's held numerous positions, and during this period of time was heavily engaged in and I might say use this term "hands on" in the negotiating process; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. He certainly was at the top of the food chain and was privy to information, conversations, briefings that you were not; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You, on the other hand, knew what you knew from the field?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you met Mr. Owen along with Mr. Andersen and it was Mr. Andersen who was the lead -- taking the lead in this instance was he was, after all, an ambassador; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At the ambassadorial level?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He basically got what we would normally call the bum's rush, the cold shoulder?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prefer the cold shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. MR. KARNAVAS: If we could go into private session for one second, Mr. President. I guess it's private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have five minutes to the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we were talking about differences of opinion, and we said that you -- you had a fixed opinion that the Croats were the aggressors. You also tell us at some point that you met a individual named Martin, Martin the monitor, who turned out to be none other than -- who was and I'm sure you recognised him at the time as Sir Martin Garrod; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I take it, since he's a sir, it must mean something, that he's pretty important.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was he at the time a major or a colonel or a general?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: A rather seasoned general at that; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A retired seasoned general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Been around, seen a lot, and you would agree with me that he's a rather respectable individual, is he not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could look at document 1D 00815. Now, Sir Martin -- while we're looking that up, Sir Martin Garrod came in at some latter point while you were in your mission and stayed on afterwards?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And from reading -- as I understand it, when you met him he was rather interested in listening to whatever you had to say and was pumping you for information.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Because, after all, he was the new boy on the block, as it were, and you were the old hand, and he wanted the benefit of your understanding of the events; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you were more than pleased to offer him, after all a general, a retired general, and of course you were there for that particular reason; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was there for which reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you were there to monitor and pass on information.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not necessarily to please a general because he was a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, no, not to please a general. But you were more than pleased to offer your insight.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was important to do it. Pleasing doesn't come into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. If we could look at -- it's page number 3 on this particular document, or it's numbered 3, and if we look at paragraph 20. I'll start reading to save some time. It says, "Throughout the last six months it has been evident that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were desperate for peace though not at any price. They continually stressed that it was they who first signed up to the Vance-Owen Plan and to the Stoltenberg Owen proposals at Geneva. They were consistently critical of the west for 'not understanding them' and for branding them as aggressors, while calling the Muslims, whom they looked upon as the aggressors, the victims. Their morale was not high throughout this period, as they saw the areas controlled by the Croats, particularly in Central Bosnia, gradually diminishing as a result of success by the BiH army." Now, here he seems to indicate that the Croats are desperate for peace. This, incidentally, this document, is generated -- if we look at the very first page. it says "18 April 1994". So it seems that he was there longer than you, and he seems, at least in this little passage, to have derived somewhat of a different opinion, that they were desperate for peace.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He made those comments quite possibly because HVO resources were stretched to the limit, exhausted, and they were indeed desperate for peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, you indicate at one point that it was a land grab both -- on all sides. They were trying to grab land. You make that reference, do you not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Because it was quite obvious, as I understand it and as you understood it at the time, that land was not going to be appropriated at the negotiating table, but all parties had to more or less negotiate based on what they had at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it would behoove not just the Croats but also the Muslims to have as much land as possible, because if in the eventuality, as the way the negotiations were proceeding, you would have a federation, you would have regions; the more land, the bigger the regions within the greater context of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whilst we might understand why they wished to do that, it doesn't mean to say we condone it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether you condoned it. I'm asking you whether that was in fact the case, because that would at least explain not just the what the Croats were doing but also what the Muslims were also doing.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I just wish to be clear with my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So what is the answer to my question? Were not the Muslims also seeking to have as much land as possible prior to -- or during the negotiating sessions so that at least if there was a confederation, as was being negotiated, they would control as much land as possible? Is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possibly, though I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you got into -- when you got to -- to Bosnia and Herzegovina back in 1993, January 8, by that point an incident had occurred much earlier in a place called Jajce; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Jajce. Jajce. Now, ECMM was not there at the time.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: ECMM observed the withdrawal from it but were not present in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you were told of those events, were you not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what you were told was, at least -- both sides blamed each other; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the Croats especially were rather upset because they felt that their allies, the ones that they had helped and protected, particularly in the Mostar area but in other areas as well, had let them down, had abandoned that area, and as a result what you had was a humanitarian crisis of about 30.000 refugees; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And about 20.000 of those refugees ended up in areas -- in the surrounding areas; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course the question was what to do with all of these -- what to do with all of these refugees.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, for the -- for the Muslims, for Izetbegovic at least, is it not a fair assumption to say that this incident of Jajce and not, say, Gornji Vakuf in January 15, 1995, as the Prosecutor would have us believe, is perhaps a key event in the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be. I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at it this way: Alija Izetbegovic has a humanitarian crisis in the sense of what to do with about 20.000 Muslims, his people, in this area; right? That's one way of looking at it.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Another way of looking at it is it also presents a serendipitous opportunity to fill in the ranks of the ABiH and also to have a rather mobile force of Muslim fighters because among those 20.000 you had -- you had also men of military age; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And of course if you are a Croat and a minority in that area, you might feel somewhat uncomfortable at having all of these refugees, especially military-aged fighters in this area; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And of course we talked a little bit earlier -

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could have just a couple of minutes, Your Honour, just to round off this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is why I went into the Territorial Defence, you see. The Territorial Defence is -- at the local territory you would have a unit available for defensive or offensive purposes, but now Alija Izetbegovic's provided with the opportunity to have a mobile unit of Muslim fighters that could go beyond and into areas for offensive purposes. And so if we look at the greater context of it, is it not, sir, possible that the situation in Jajce was a lot more significant and more important than perhaps the ECMM understood it to be because of the humanitarian crisis, because they provided the Muslims with a mobile army plus they increased whatever army that they had, plus because of the land grab, keeping in mind when we come back from the break I'm going to have a few questions on the negotiations that had been ongoing which demonstrate that the regionalisation process was already not just mere -- a mere thought but it was something that was being negotiated. So is it a fact, sir, is it possible that perhaps you and your -- and others in ECMM simply did not understand the significance of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an event that had happened. One was to see what the outcome would be. It was not for me to foretell it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you, sir, make any efforts to really understand -- one question. One question. Did you make any efforts, sir, you or ECMM, or did you get any briefing papers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Karnavas, you just asked a question numbering several lines. He answered, but if you would like to, you can take it up again after the break. We have to stop. It's to twenty to 6.00, and we will reconvene at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be heard just for one moment. Mr. Karnavas has indicated that he proposes to continue his cross- examination after the break that we've just had, and I understand that he has many questions to put in his client's interests. I just feel, Your Honour, that I should go on the record at this time as pointing out that this witness testified about our client, Mr. Stojic, and it is necessary for us also to cross-examine him at some length, and I thought that we had made this clear to other counsel. But for the record, Ms. Nozica and I have divided the labour of cross-examination between us. Because of cross- examination by other counsel, what I have to do has been reduced probably by about three-quarters, so I can be very brief. But our best estimate is that we are going to require two hours of cross-examination approximately, and I know that that, therefore, has consequences for Mr. Kovacic, and he may also wish to go on the record at this time. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kovacic, how much time will you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, after the questions put by other Defence counsel to avoid repetition, I feel that we will need up to two hours. I see no way of reducing this further in view of the number of documents used with this witness, and especially bearing in mine

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: document, taking up four or five hours of testimony. This is basically the written statement of the witness, and by tendering the document, the Prosecutor has saved himself four or five hours of examination time. However, it requires cross-examination. If I may add, Your Honours, and it's quite reasonable for Your Honours to be concerned about this, the Prosecutor has envisaged two and a half hours for the next witness, which means that if the Prosecutor starts at the end of the day tomorrow or doesn't start tomorrow, he will have the whole day for that witness on the following day, Thursday. This witness is a brief witness, and he has been scheduled to take two and a half hours. So we ask Your Honours to grant us the two hours we need for this witness, because we cannot cross-examine on this volume of documents in less. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be heard. I need -- over the break while others were relaxes I looked at my notes. I need five minutes to wrap it up. I can understand Mr. Murphy's discontent, but I represent a client, too, as he does, and so -- and I'm sure there are going to be times when he's going to need more time and I'm just going to have to bite the bullet. But be that as it may, just five minutes, Your Honour, that's all I need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you will need five minutes. The registrar told me earlier on that we've used up seven hours and 44 minutes. So the Defence has used up seven hours and 44 minutes. This will go beyond the 10-hour mark. If I understand correctly, you need five more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That means that the following counsel will have 45 minutes. So we can still make it. So please round off your cross-examination quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, if we could talk a little bit about the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and your efforts on the ground, just very briefly. When you came in theatre, you had no prior experience in government; correct? In running a government.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And part of your job over there, you were not responsible for the -- for the safety of anyone in a sense, the local people? Well, you were not there to protect them; right? You were there to monitor.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were not responsible to make sure that they had running water or electricity or that pensions were paid or taxes were collected to pay for everyday life; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there to report if they didn't have --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether you were there to report it. Please just answer the question. You weren't there -- when you were there, you were not responsible to make sure that the electricity was running, the water was running, the garbage was picked up, that normal life could go on?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Others were; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated and you indicate that Mr. Prlic had a different view than you did, right, on how to go about implementation? Right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. It was your understanding, as it was the understanding of the ECMM, that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was going forward, and in fact you indicated that you had been given instructions by the ECMM to assist in the implementation; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But other than being told go ahead, you weren't given a blueprint; you weren't given any information, detailed information, on how to go about implementing this peace plan; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in your conversation with Mr. Prlic, he had indicated what he thought was necessary; correct? At least how to proceed; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To a degree. All right. And in fact, one of the things that he asked you to do is to try to find the opposite interlocutor so he could begin this process with perhaps you participating in it; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course we've talked about - you've indicated on the record - that finding the right, appropriate Muslim interlocutor was always a problem because one -- correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Prlic never presented to you a fait accompli; in other words, a take-it-or-leave-it package, this is it, it's intractable, this is what has to be implemented. But, rather, his approach was, "This is how I think we should proceed. Bring me this interlocutor and let's talk." Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you would expect him, representing his interest, he would try to present a package at least as a starting point that would be as favourable as possible to the Croats, and you would expect the Muslims to do the same; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So that's the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. We've covered that briefly. Just one last issue. I know it's going to be covered in great detail, but since you mentioned my client with respect to this, I need to ask you a question or two. The issue of the Mujahedin. As I understand it from reading what has been -- what you have written, you indicate that when you went to Zenica, you became aware of the so-called Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact nobody wanted to take credit of who they were under; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But it was very clear that they were part of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, you indicate that you were rather cautious and didn't want to go into too much -- you didn't want to explore too much as to who they were, what they were doing, because of your own safety; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. And in fact, you discussed that. And at some point, as I indicate -- as I understand it, you were afraid that you would be kidnapped by these people, not by Croats but kidnapped by these Mujahedin types; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a consideration, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But you were there to monitor, were you not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And monitoring would require, would it not, for you to actually, not just you but others, to actually go in and explore and to find out whether in fact, you know, they were foreign fighters, Arab extremists perhaps, Mujahedin, whatever you want to call them, and to report accurately and completely as you were required to do; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But in this instance at least, for safety reasons, because after all the Muslims were afraid of these foreign fighters, these Mujahedin, you didn't make as many -- you didn't make the required efforts, perhaps, that would have been necessary. So at least today you could say yes, there were Mujahedin; this was the number; this is where they came from, and so on and so forth. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. We had very few resources. We had very many leads to follow up. It was only actually physically possible in 24 hours to follow up a certain number of leads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people in the mission who did look closely at what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But nonetheless, in what you've written and in what you've stated, you seem to downgrade and almost denigrate if not outright dismiss what you had been hearing from the Croats, including Mr. Prlic, that there were Mujahedin extremists out there and that they had been committing crimes; correct? I mean, one gets that impression.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely. That they may have committed some crimes. All parties may have committed some crimes at a certain level. That's quite different from the shelling of communities and outright infantry attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Praljak is going to inform you about all of that. Just finally one last question. If we could go into private session, Your Honour, just for one second. I know it takes a second to get in there.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, wait a moment. There's another question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I apologise to Mr. Murphy, not allowing him to speak, but I would like to share with you my preoccupation about the time that's used now. We all recall that there was a decision by the Trial Chamber, which was of course also accepted and confirmed by the Appeals Chamber, about the time to be used by the Prosecution and also by the distinguished team of Defence, and I would like to recall that this issue was many times raised. I am afraid, and I have to speak about it quite clearly but emphatically, that now we are going to lose too much time if we are going - - if that approach will be continued. I suggested to the President, the Presiding Judge Antonetti, and he graciously agreed, that we have to look into the ratio of the time used by the Prosecution and the Defence, and we have to come back to this question soon, because we would like to go ahead with a certain amount of diligence. At the same time, of course, give the possibility to the Defence time to do its work, but at the same time we have to be in conformity with the rules which we have established. So this being said, I would like, of course, I would like to thank you for listening to me and I would like to ask the Defence to cooperate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, if I could just for one -- for one very brief moment. I've raised this issue with at least one of the Defence teams. There could very well be a number of issues particularly relating to the Mujahedin that the Prosecution would be prepared to stipulate and agree to. Some of these issues that the Defence are planning on cross-examining are not at issue necessarily in this case in our position and are clearly going to be things that we would be prepared to agree to, and I would perhaps rather than spending several hours tomorrow on the Mujahedin again invite the Defence teams to put in writing specific issues that they would propose, and Mr. Scott and I, with our team, will sit down and see whether these are really issues that are live issues in this case. Clearly as this Trial Chamber is well aware, this institution has indicted crimes committed by the Mujahedin, allegedly committed by the Mujahedin. We're not disputing that there were crimes committed by the Mujahedin. But what we need to see are some specific and concrete proposals by the Defence as to things that they believe are relevant and we are prepared to sit down and look at those issues to see if there's agreement. We do not believe that several hours of cross-examination of this witness or any other witness on the issue of crimes committed by the Mujahedin are in the best interests of anyone involved in this case and simply will result in prolonging this case. Many of these issues I don't believe are going to actually be in dispute. I would invite the Defence teams to seriously sit down with us and propose things in writing in advance so that we can review them, and this should be a way of eliminating a huge amount of time concerning the issue of the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber hopes that the Defence counsel have heard Mr. Mundis's proposal. We invite you to meet, because it's -- it would be a waste of time for you to ask -- to ask questions during cross-examination, whereas the Prosecution fully agrees with your position. You have about three-quarters of an hour left, Mr. Murphy. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I just check that we are in public session? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Beese.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I just have a relatively few questions for you on behalf of Mr. Bruno Stojic. I'm going to try to go slowly as I appreciate you have also to enable the interpreters to catch up with us. You gave evidence that you had a number of meetings with Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And the purpose of these meetings was to facilitate your being able to get to certain locations.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You understood that Mr. Stojic was the person that you had to go to to get permission for certain activities.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To his office, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: By the time you arrived in theatre, Herceg-Bosna was an established reality, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, let me rephrase that question then. The officials of Herceg-Bosna were people with whom you had to deal in order to carry out your functions.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officials of the HVO rather than Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, were you -- were you aware of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: As a concept.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: How many -- on how many occasions total -- in total did you meet with Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe about five.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And after that, I understand it became more the practice for you to meet with his deputy, Mr. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And if you can answer this in a meaningful way, on the occasions you met with Mr. Stojic, about how long would those meetings last?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 15 minutes, half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, you gave evidence about a meeting that occurred on or about the 18th of April, 1993. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And that was a meeting where Mr. Ganic was present?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And you recorded that at some point during that meeting, Mr. Stojic gave -- gave something of what you call, I think, a tirade to Mr. Ganic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was not in the room at the time when he arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But you understood that Mr. Stojic had expressed himself forcibly to Mr. Ganic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: About what he saw as certain crimes or atrocities committed by Muslims against Croat victims.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And it was your understanding that Mr. Stojic was angry about that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: That's understandable, is it not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In fact, sir, you during your army career served in Northern Ireland, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER BEESE [Resumed]
